metadata.title: Is the “Net Generation” Ready for Digital Citizenship? Perspectives from the IEA International Computer and Information Literacy Study 2013

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This policy brief summarizes results from ICILS 2013, which used a multi-stage sampling design of Grade 8 (or equivalent) students within participating education systems and schools. The brief reports descriptive percentages and an international CIL achievement scale, but it does not specify whether analysts applied ICILS student/sampling weights or replicate weights in the computations presented here. Because the document is a secondary policy synthesis rather than a methods section, the exact weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) and variance estimation approach are not documented. For any re-analysis using ICILS microdata, analysts should apply the official ICILS sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the international database to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The brief does not present an original student-level predictive modeling analysis with an explicitly stated plausible-values (PV) workflow; instead, it reports high-level ICILS findings (e.g., percentages of students meeting CIL tasks and differences on an international CIL achievement scale). As a result, PV handling and missing-data procedures are not described in this policy brief. This is a reporting/secondary-synthesis limitation: the underlying ICILS technical documentation would be required to determine the exact PV combination rules and missing-data treatment used to produce the reported CIL scale results.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief states that ICILS focused on Grade 8 (or equivalent) students and that just under 60,000 Grade 8 (or equivalent) students from more than 3,300 schools across 21 education systems participated. It does not describe additional analytic exclusions (e.g., task completion thresholds, missing background-variable rules) for the specific percentages and scale differences reported in this policy brief. Therefore, the filtering criteria for the analytic results shown here are not specified beyond the Grade 8 (or equivalent) and participating education systems scope.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief synthesizes findings from ICILS 2013, which assessed Grade 8 (or equivalent) students’ computer and information literacy (CIL) across 21 education systems. The underlying ICILS assessment used a four-part framework covering individual learner skills and contextual factors in home, in-school, and wider community settings, with contextual questionnaires also collected from around 35,000 teachers and additional school ICT-related staff. The brief reports that, on average across participating systems, only about a quarter of students could identify characteristics of an untrustworthy email and about a fifth could recognize biased or unreliable information, indicating limited critical use of digital information. It also highlights large cross-country variation in home access to computers and internet, and it reports that teacher confidence and ICT integration beyond basic tasks are limited. The policy implications emphasize targeted CIL instruction, alignment of in-school and out-of-school ICT use, and investment in teacher education and professional development.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy brief that summarizes ICILS 2013 results rather than presenting an original empirical ML analysis with a specified modeling pipeline, PV combination rules, missing-data strategy, or per-country analytic sample sizes. Consequently, fields that would normally be extracted from a methods/results section for an ML paper (e.g., ML algorithms, model performance metrics, and PV handling details) are not available in the provided text. The extraction therefore focuses on the assessment scope (Grade 8, 21 education systems, sample size) and the reported descriptive/scale findings used to motivate policy recommendations.
